text: This lesson covers BULK COLLECT and FORALL, two performance-oriented features built specifically to cut down the overhead of row by row processing in PL-SQL.

Here's the problem they solve. Every time PL-SQL hands a statement to the SQL engine and gets control back, that's a context switch, and it carries real overhead. A cursor loop that fetches one row, then runs one update, then fetches the next, repeats that switch thousands of times across a large result set.

BULK COLLECT fixes the fetch side. Select employee I-D, bulk collect into a collection, from employees, where department equals ninety. That pulls the entire result set into memory in a single context switch, instead of one switch per row the way an ordinary fetch loop works.

FORALL fixes the DML side. For all, I in v ids dot first through v ids dot last, update employees — this sends a whole batch of update statements, one per collection element, to the SQL engine as a single bulk operation, instead of looping through them one at a time.

Put BULK COLLECT and FORALL together, and this technique has a real name: bulk binding. It's one of the most widely documented, genuinely real PL-SQL performance recommendations there is — Oracle's own guidance points developers toward it constantly, not some obscure trick.

And if this feels familiar, it should: it's the exact same reasoning behind a T-SQL habit you probably already have, preferring a set based insert select, or a table valued parameter, over looping through rows with a cursor. Next lesson is the chapter's capstone: translating a real T-SQL stored procedure into PL-SQL, line by line, calling out every decision point along the way. See you there.
